system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Quasi-threshold editing
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Quasi-threshold graphs as skeleton forests, QTM, the simple-path lemmas, and local optimality via path sorting. Includes the resulting linear-time inclusion-minimal editing and its streaming interpretation.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C04-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: In a quasi-threshold graph with skeleton forest T, an edge {u,v} exists if and only if u and v are in an ancestor-descendant relationship in T.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0151-s15] If u and v are on the same simple path, N[u] = N[v]: An edge {u,v} exists if and only if u and v are in an ancestor-descendant relationship in the skeleton T.
- CS-ALG-C04-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Quasi-threshold editing yields a partition of a graph into communities and, for each community, a centralized nesting structure that is represented by its skeleton tree.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0149-s07] Quasi-threshold editing yields a partition into communities and in addition for each of them a centralized nesting structure repre- sented by their skeleton tree.
- CS-ALG-C04-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Threshold graphs are the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs, and they form a subclass of quasi-threshold graphs.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0149-s03] Threshold graphs are the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs and therefore a subclass of quasi- threshold graphs.
- CS-ALG-C04-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Incrementally inserting the nodes of a graph G into an initially empty graph with the QTM local moving routine yields an inclusion-minimal editing of G, because each step minimizes the number of edits.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0153-s13] With the local moving routine of QTM, we can incrementally insert the nodes of a graph G into an initially empty graph.
    [CS-ALG-p0153-s14] Due to Lemma 4, this minimizes the number of edits in each step.
    [CS-ALG-p0153-s15] Overall, this yields an inclusion-minimal editing of G, as it has also been shown, e.g., for interval graphs [26].
- CS-ALG-C04-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Applying QTM to a node u on the skeleton forest with u removed and simple paths reordered so that the neighbors of u are at the top of their simple paths minimizes the number of edits incident to u.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0152-s16] Apply- ing QTM to u on T −which is T with u removed and simple paths reordered such that neighbors of u are at the top of their simple paths minimizes the number of edits incident to u.
- CS-ALG-C04-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: When the Quasi-Threshold Mover (QTM) moves a node u, in the induced quasi-threshold graph u is adjacent to the new parent v, v's ancestors, and the adopted children with their descendants. Each neighbor of u among these nodes saves deleting an edge, each non-neighbor requires inserting an edge, and QTM selects the parent and adopted children that maximize the number of u-neighbors minus non-neighbors.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s04] In the induced quasi-threshold graph, u is then connected to v and all its ancestors as well as to all adopted children and their descendants.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s05] Every neighbor x of u in this set of nodes saves deleting the edges {u,x} but every non-neighbor y of u implies inserting the edge {u,y}.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s06] Therefore, we select the parent v and the children to adopt such that the number of u- neighbors minus non-neighbors is maximized.
- CS-ALG-C04-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: When QTM moves node u, neighbors of u at depth greater than $2 \times \deg(u)$ can be ignored, because connecting u to such a neighbor would force at least $\deg(u)+1$ edge insertions, whereas making u a root causes only $\deg(u)$ edits.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s27] Consider a node v ∈N(u) with depth larger than 2 × deg(u).
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s28] If u is connected to v in the edited graph, this implies that u is also connected to all at least 2 × deg(u) ancestors of u.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s29] Among these, there can be at most the remaining deg(u) −1 neighbors and thus at least deg(u)+1 non-neighbors.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s30] Thus, this implies deg(u)+1 edge insertions.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s31] Making u a root in the forest, i.e., deleting all edges incident to u, causes just deg(u) edits and is thus better.
- CS-ALG-C04-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The one-pass streaming reading of inclusion-minimal editing requires that, whenever a node u is encountered in the stream, all edges between u and the already seen nodes are also supplied.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0153-s17] This inclusion-minimal editing algorithm can also be considered a one-pass stream- ing algorithm.
    [CS-ALG-p0153-s19] We only consider the edges of every node once, the only constraint is that when we encounter a node u in the stream, we also need to get all incident edges that are incident to the already seen nodes.
- CS-ALG-C04-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Reordering nodes within simple paths is the only way a skeleton forest can be modified without changing the quasi-threshold graph it induces.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0151-s05] A crucial observation is that reordering nodes in simple paths is the only way the skeleton forest can be modiﬁed without affecting the induced quasi-threshold graph.
- CS-ALG-C04-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: QTM can ignore neighbors of $u$ at depth greater than $2\times\deg(u)$. Connecting $u$ to such a neighbor would force at least $\deg(u)+1$ edge insertions, whereas making $u$ a root costs only $\deg(u)$ edits.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s26] More precisely, we show that we can ignore neighbors at a depth of more than 2 × deg(u).
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s27] Consider a node v ∈N(u) with depth larger than 2 × deg(u).
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s28] If u is connected to v in the edited graph, this implies that u is also connected to all at least 2 × deg(u) ancestors of u.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s29] Among these, there can be at most the remaining deg(u) −1 neighbors and thus at least deg(u)+1 non-neighbors.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s30] Thus, this implies deg(u)+1 edge insertions.
    [CS-ALG-p0150-s31] Making u a root in the forest, i.e., deleting all edges incident to u, causes just deg(u) edits and is thus better.
